name: BMW M5 (E60)
transmission: 7-speed SMG III single-clutch automated manual at US launch; a rare 6-speed manual was added for the US in 2007 (US was the only market to get the 6MT)
0_to_60: ~4.5 sec (BMW quote; instrumented tests often ~4.1–4.3 sec)
reliability: 6/10 — the E60 M5 is a technological high-water mark: the only V10 M5, an F1-inspired 5.0L revving past 8,000 rpm to 500 hp. It is also the most demanding M5 to own. The S85's undersized rod bearings need replacement roughly every 60k–80k miles or the engine can grenade; the two throttle actuators wear out on nearly every car; and the SMG III's hydraulic pump and clutch are consumables. None of this is a deal-breaker for an owner who budgets for it — but this is a car you maintain to a schedule and a bank balance, not one you neglect.
cost_to_own: Insurance: High · Maintenance ~$2,500+/yr realistically (rod bearings, throttle actuators, SMG pump/clutch, thirst) · Buy the best-maintained car you can find; a cheap E60 M5 is the most expensive kind
popular_mods: Preventive rod-bearing replacement (upgraded bearings) — non-negotiable insurance on an S85
Rebuilt or replacement throttle actuators before they fail and force limp mode
An SMG pump/accumulator refresh and clutch service on SMG cars
A software/exhaust freshening to enjoy the V10's top end (leave the engine internals stock)
Honest take: the smartest 'mods' are preventive rod bearings, throttle actuators, and SMG service — reliability is the whole game on an E60 M5
oil_interval: Every ~3,000–5,000 miles (well short of BMW's default — critical for protecting the rod bearings)

generations.E60 M5 (2006–2010 US): BMW M's most extreme M5 — a naturally-aspirated 5.0L V10 with individual throttle bodies and adjustable P400/P500 power modes, paired at launch with the SMG III automated manual. Ferocious top-end performance and drama, at the cost of complexity and thirst.
generations.6-speed manual (US-only, 2007+): A conventional Getrag 6-speed manual was offered only in the US market — rare, desirable, and the way to skip the SMG's pump/clutch headaches (though the engine's rod-bearing needs are unchanged).

common_issues: Rod-bearing failure — undersized bearings/clearances for a high-revving V10; replace every ~60k–80k miles
Throttle-actuator failure — the two bank-mounted actuators wear out on nearly every S85 eventually
SMG hydraulic pump failure and clutch wear (clutch is a ~30k–50k mile consumable)
VANOS faults, sometimes triggered by rod-bearing debris
High oil consumption and expensive routine maintenance overall
maintenance_tips: Shorten oil changes to ~3,000–5,000 miles with the correct 10W-60 to protect the bearings
Treat rod bearings as scheduled maintenance, not a repair — replace preventively on interval
Budget for throttle actuators and, on SMG cars, the pump and clutch
Buy on documented history above all — service records are worth more than low mileage here
Let the V10 fully warm before using the upper rev range

engine.detail: The S85 — a 5.0L naturally-aspirated V10 revving to ~8,250 rpm for 500 hp and 383 lb-ft at 6,100 rpm, with individual throttle bodies, double-VANOS, and selectable P400/P500 power modes. An F1-inspired high-water mark and the only V10 M5.
engine.watch: The defining flaw is undersized rod bearings — replace roughly every 60k-80k miles or the engine can grenade (short 10W-60 oil changes help). Also expect high oil consumption and VANOS faults, sometimes triggered by rod-bearing debris.

drivetrain.detail: 7-speed SMG III single-clutch automated manual at US launch, or the rare US-only 2007+ Getrag 6-speed manual, sending power to the rear wheels through a limited-slip differential.
drivetrain.watch: On SMG cars the hydraulic pump can fail and the clutch is a ~30k-50k mile consumable — the 6MT skips those headaches, though not the engine's rod-bearing needs.

suspension.detail: Aluminum front strut and rear multilink with Electronic Damping Control (EDC) — composed and quick for a ~4,012 lb sedan.
suspension.watch: Age-related bushing and EDC damper wear soften body control; refresh on high-mile cars to bring it back.

brakes.detail: Large vented discs sized to haul a heavy sedan down from V10 speeds, repeatedly.
brakes.watch: Effective but expensive — rotors, pads, and fluid are pricey consumables, especially with any track use.

electrical.detail: Two bank-mounted electric throttle actuators drive the individual throttle bodies, and the car is dense with electronics (iDrive, SMG hydraulic control).
electrical.watch: The throttle actuators wear out on nearly every S85 and will drop the car into limp mode — rebuilt or replacement units are a near-inevitable job. Treat it as budgeted maintenance.

body.detail: Steel unibody sedan (a Touring wagon was sold abroad) — a discreet, full-size Q-ship.
body.watch: Structurally solid; the real 'body' issue is financial — a cheap E60 M5 hides a heavy maintenance bill and is the most expensive kind to own. Buy on documented history above all.
